Rural households are facing higher price pressures than their urban counterparts.MoSPI data show that rural inflation climbed to 6.63% in October, compared with 5.41% in urban areas. Food inflation was also higher in rural India at 9.09%, against 8.68% in urban India.The difference matters because food purchases form a regular and unavoidable part of household spending. Higher prices can therefore put pressure on rural budgets even when the overall national inflation number appears relatively moderate.(function(){function e(){window.addEventListener(`message`,function(e){if(e.data[`datawrapper-height`]!==void 0){var t=document.querySelectorAll(`iframe`);for(var n in e.data[`datawrapper-height`])for(var r=0,i;i=t[r];r++)if(i.contentWindow===e.source){var a=e.data[`datawrapper-height`][n]+`px`;i.style.height=a}}})}e()})();There are also considerable differences across states. Among states, Tamil Nadu recorded the highest combined retail inflation at 7.29% in October. Telangana followed at 7.26%, Andhra Pradesh at 7.25%, Madhya Pradesh at 7.19% and Odisha at 7.17%.Puducherry, a Union Territory, recorded an even higher rate of 7.96%. At the other end, Delhi's combined inflation stood at 3.80%.These differences show why the experience of inflation can vary depending on where a household lives. The national figure is an average, but the actual price pressure depends on the items people buy and the local markets they depend on.(function(){function e(){window.addEventListener(`message`,function(e){if(e.data[`datawrapper-height`]!==void 0){var t=document.querySelectorAll(`iframe`);for(var n in e.data[`datawrapper-height`])for(var r=0,i;i=t[r];r++)if(i.contentWindow===e.source){var a=e.data[`datawrapper-height`][n]+`px`;i.style.height=a}}})}e()})();Are salaries keeping up with rising prices?As everyday expenses continue to rise, a salary hike can feel like a welcome relief, offering some cushion against bigger bills. But once the monthly expenses are paid, the extra money may not leave as much in your pocket as you had expected.According to Aon's salary increase survey, India Inc was expected to offer average salary hikes of 9.1% in 2026, compared with 8.9% in 2025. On paper, that may look like a decent cushion against rising prices. But does it really stretch far enough?For starters, these are only averages, and not everyone gets the same pay rise. The real impact also depends on where a household spends most of its money. Grant Thornton Bharat's India's Financial Resilience Report 2026 found that 62% of respondents believe their income growth will not be enough to keep pace with future inflation. Among those aged 25-34, the share was even higher at 70%.Tripathi says incomes have broadly held up over the past year, although the picture varies across employees. Government employees received dearness allowance revisions linked to inflation, while private-sector salary hikes depended on performance and individual outcomes. However, when household budgets get tighter, families often cut back on discretionary spending to protect essentials. As he puts it, “Essentials were protected, and 'wants' were cut.”So, will a salary hike really make you richer? Not necessarily. What matters is how much you can retain after meeting your monthly expenses. For instance, even a 5% reduction in a household's monthly budget of Rs 50,000 can free up Rs 2,500 a month, or Rs 30,000 annually.Adhil Shetty, CEO of BankBazaar, says households should focus on protecting their cash flow without compromising long-term financial security. “When prices rise faster than income, the first thing that tends to help is building a buffer, roughly a few months of expenses kept aside for emergencies,” he said.He also recommends maintaining an emergency fund covering 3-6 months of essential expenses, prioritising repayment of high-interest debt and reviewing regular spending to identify costs that may have quietly crept up.Ultimately, it is not just about how much extra money lands in your payslip, but how much is left after groceries, bills and other everyday needs. The biggest risk is quietly sacrificing tomorrow's savings to maintain yesterday's lifestyle.Breather or burden: Will prices finally cool down?Will your grocery bills finally give you some breathing room, or is more price trouble waiting around the corner? The answer will depend on food supplies, farm output and global commodity prices over the next few months.Fresh winter crop arrivals could help bring down prices of some food items. However, global fuel prices and transportation costs could continue to keep everyday goods expensive.Shetty says stable global commodity prices and better agricultural output could help inflation cool gradually. Tripathi, meanwhile, believes the current price pressure is largely supply-driven. He points out that raising interest rates cannot directly bring down crude oil prices or freight charges.“Higher interest rates can cool demand, but they cannot lower the cost of crude oil or reduce freight charges,” Tripathi says. In his view, cheaper fuel and smoother supplies are key to easing the pressure.Relief on two frontsBringing down the cost of everyday essentials and leaving households with more money to spend will both be important.In the short term, better food supplies, improved stock management and targeted support for vulnerable households can help ease the burden. Over the longer term, investments in cold storage, farm-to-market transport and agricultural productivity can help prevent sudden price spikes.Singh says relief needs to address both essential costs and household incomes. “Targeted food supply interventions, better inventory management and focused support for vulnerable households can ease pressure,” he says.While targeted support can reach households within weeks, these structural improvements will take longer to deliver results.Ultimately, real relief from inflation is not just about a lower number on paper. It means being able to buy everyday essentials, pay the bills and still have enough left to save, without constantly having to reshuffle the monthly budget.Money habits form by age 7. articles.title: Why tech bros are desperate to bring Jensen Huang back — and why that would be a mistake
articles.summary: Silicon Valley wants its moneymaker-in-chief back.
articles.body: Silicon Valley wants its moneymaker-in-chief back. Jensen Huang, forced to resign from Nvidia last week in the midst of multiple scandals, has found a groundswell of support for his unlikely return. Among the cheerleaders for Huang’s comeback: several prominent Big Tech executives and the president of the United States. Their desire for his reinstatement is plain: Nvidia is the AI industry’s financier, and Jensen Huang the top dealmaker. Nvidia’s willingness to lend gobs of money to AI companies to help make their massive ambitions possible turned Huang into the king of AI. Still, some of Huang’s more questionable deals – and his questionable behavior – also put the company at risk. Huang’s actions punctured massive holes in the myth of his singular and irreplaceable leadership, surfacing some significant preexisting doubts about the viability of the company’s long-term business strategy. A more conservative Nvidia – one that plays by the rules – may be painful for AI companies that relied on Huang’s risktaking in the near term. But it could set Nvidia and the broader industry on a more sustainable course in the long run. How Nvidia made the AI industry rich Around 200,000 signatories of a #standwithjensen open letter argued Huang deserves to come back to Nvidia, at least while an independent investigation continues. Many of the comments defended Huang as indispensable and the linchpin of the AI industry’s success. Nvidia declined to comment. Huang engendered support from the industry by spearheading complicated financing deals – often called circular financing – that gave many AI companies access to Nvidia’s powerful chips and computing power that they wouldn’t otherwise be able to afford or access. The amount of money involved in those deals is astounding: Nvidia last quarter listed $164.5 billion in land and power guarantees and AI cloud infrastructure agreements, including $20 billion worth of leases for data centers that haven’t broken ground yet. Nvidia isn’t just financing small companies: Included in that sum is $105 billion in leases to SB Energy, a company with backing from SoftBank that is building a massive Ohio data center for OpenAI. In turn, that massive funding secured demand for Nvidia’s own products – and stakes in the companies that bought or leased its chips: Nvidia owns about $3 billion worth of SB Energy’s shares – and $45 billion worth of other companies’ stock. Huang’s ouster could take $50 billion out of the circular financing system, according to Tim Arcuri, analyst at UBS. The Asia conundrum Another risk of Huang’s ouster: New leadership will probably be more cautious about where and with whom it does business, particularly in Southeast Asia. Huang knew the company needed the region to support Nvidia’s ambitious growth targets. He championed Nvidia’s ability to continue selling its chips to China, despite US export restrictions – ultimately gaining the Trump administration’s support to carve out a path for the company to sell powerful, but not top-tier, AI chips there. Ironically, Huang’s scandal may put some of Nvidia’s access to the region at risk. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Sunday told Fox News that the company’s international sales merit more scrutiny. “Were they pressing these seemingly illicit sales to goose their revenues and their earnings?” Bessent wondered aloud. The dynamics of Jensen Huang’s relationship to Megaspeed’s Alice Huang remain uncertain, as is her potential role as a Chinese intelligence asset. But the Singaporean government and US officials have been scrutinizing Megaspeed for potentially reselling Nvidia’s chips to unauthorized Chinese buyers. Nvidia’s board on Tuesday sait it had established a new national security and export control oversight committee that will meet at least quarterly and ensure the company is abiding by global trade regulations. It will also beef up its internal national security and compliance initiatives. The US Commerce Department on Monday proposed tightened restrictions on sales of high-end AI chips to Singapore following the scandal. Reduced sales to Singapore and other Southeast Asian countries could risk as much as a 10% reduction to Nvidia’s revenue in the long term, said Arcuri. An Nvidia without Huang Despite those risks, Huang’s ouster may ultimately make for a strong Nvidia. Those so-called circular financing deals are controversial for a reason: The deals can leave Nvidia on the hook if a borrower defaults, a data center project is severely delayed or demand for AI falls through. Across the industry, the value of those off-balance-sheet debt obligations, including long-term contracts and lease guarantees, exceeds $3 trillion, said Federal Reserve Governor Michael Barr in a speech Monday. He noted rising bond yields for smaller AI companies led to increasingly complex deals that warrant particularly close scrutiny and could mess with the market. “This financial complexity can be opaque,” Barr said. “That opacity can exacerbate selloffs when investor sentiment shifts, as it is hard to know where risk resides.” Nvidia’s interim CEO Colette Kress, who is the company’s chief financial officer, had challenged Huang on some of the more audacious funding efforts, including increasingly controversial and highly leveraged neocloud companies, noted Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, senior associate dean for leadership studies at the Yale School of Management. He believes Kress, with the support of a more cautious board, will be tempted to rein in some of Nvidia’s riskier financing operations. Tech bros and President Donald Trump may be advocating for Huang to stick around, but fears about a management shakeup impact on Nvidia are overblown, a number of industry analysts argue. Kress predicted in August that the company’s sales will grow 70% next year, and demand for Nvidia’s AI chips remains so high, the company will maintain a backlog of orders that lasts well into 2028. “Leadership does matter, particularly when you’re talking about someone as influential as Jensen Huang who has been at the helm for 33 years and is seen as a tech visionary,” said Ken Mahoney, CEO of Mahoney Asset Management. “So this is no joke, but the company certainly is not going out of business from this and investors needed to keep that in mind.” And it’s not like Huang’s scandals shine a positive light on him and his decision making. Keeping Huang in power (or bringing him back) would have been a bigger risk than letting him walk, said Nell Minow, chair of corporate governance advisory firm ValueEdge Advisors. No one can sustain the hockey stick-like growth Nvidia had exhibited over the past several years. When companies start growing exponentially, that’s when CEOs tend to start grasping at straws for new growth paths – and that’s when they often get into trouble, noted Minow. So a more discerning Nvidia adds short-term volatility but could put it on the path to greater sustainability. And it may have a better chance of achieving that without Huang. “Sad about Jensen. Shakespearean,” said former Goldman Sachs CEO Lloyd Blankfein in a post on X. “But as de Gaulle said, ‘The graveyards are filled with indispensable men.’”

articles.title: The tariff scapegoat doesn’t explain the blue wave
articles.summary: Ignore the noise — stay the course on trade.
articles.body:
In the wake of the blue tsunami election, the knives are out for the Trump tariffs. But before we throw America’s industrial future overboard, let’s look at the evidence.

Start with a remarkable study by Caroline Freund, dean of the University of California-San Diego’s School of Global Policy and Strategy. Her analysis of the 2025 tariff shock finds foreign exporters absorbed nearly half of the burden by cutting their prices.

Of course, other researchers have told a different story. A New York Fed study estimated U.S. importers shouldered 86 percent to 94 percent of the burden through November 2025. Germany’s Kiel Institute put the domestic share at 96 percent.

Yet Freund identifies a critical distinction: Those studies tend to treat tiny product-country trade relationships much like enormous ones. She corrects for this by weighting trade by economic value , and her study covers the 50 largest U.S. trading partners, accounting for more than 95 percent of U.S. goods imports.

Freund’s underlying insight is that dominant exporters, unlike marginal suppliers, have margins and market share to defend and cut prices accordingly as tariffs rise. That is consistent with what President Trump and I have been saying for years: Big exporters like China, Vietnam, and Europe depend so heavily on the U.S. market that they eat much of the tariffs through price cuts.

Consider Freund’s examples . Chinese toy and doll exporters, facing a 28-percentage-point tariff increase, cut prices by 22 percent. South Korean automakers, facing a 22-point increase, cut prices 12 percent. Indian cotton bedsheet producers, facing a 28-point increase, cut prices 16 percent.

While Freund does not find or claim that tariffs impose zero costs on Americans, her work nonetheless demolishes the anti-tariff spin that foreign exporters never absorb a meaningful share. In this way, her findings complement my own work at the White House.

Since Trump first imposed tariffs in 2018, I have seen no credible evidence that consumers have borne anything close to the full burden the critics claim. Nor is there any credible evidence that tariffs are the main driver of today’s inflation. The reason is worth repeating: big exporters like China and Europe, whose growth depends on the U.S. market, must eat much of the tariffs rather than pass them all on to consumers.

November’s exit polls explain why this debate matters politically—and why the topic is so ripe for political spin. Sixty-six percent of voters said Trump’s tariffs hurt the national economy; 79 percent said inflation caused their families moderate or severe hardship; and 89 percent called the cost of living a crucial or major factor in their vote.

Yet much of the anti-tariff sentiment that surfaced in the polling reflects a conflation of the Trump tariffs with the real inflation accelerant — the Iran energy shock, which has gasoline prices up 37 percent from a year ago.

Meanwhile, the industrial evidence is building that tariffs are catalyzing an American manufacturing renaissance. The ISM manufacturing index has remained above 50, the line that signals expansion, for ten straight months . The October jobs report brought 19,000 manufacturing jobs, bringing the 2026 gain to 101,000. Manufacturing employment is now 8,000 above its January 2025 level after last year’s decline.

Meanwhile, employment among nonresidential specialty-trade contractors, a broader category that includes workers on industrial projects, has risen nearly 120,000 since Trump took office. Equipment investment surged at a 21 percent annualized pace in the third quarter, with industrial equipment up nearly 25 percent .

Nor should we forget that tariffs produce significant revenue while changing incentives to invest here. The Office of Management and Budget internally estimates a tariff contribution of as much as $3 trillion to the Treasury over the next ten years. That is real fiscal firepower.

The lesson, then, of November’s blue tsunami is not to surrender America’s manufacturing strategy to the commentariat — or to the K Street crowd lobbying the House and Senate to hamstring the tariffs. It is that Trump’s tariffs remain a central instrument of America’s reindustrialization and manufacturing renaissance.

These Trump tariffs are not only bringing prosperity to our manufacturing heartland. By reshoring our supply chains, they are also ensuring a more secure nation. That’s the signal. Ignore the noise and stay the course.

Peter Navarro is the White House senior counselor for trade and manufacturing.

articles.title: India pays Rs 9 a GB; AI inference must be priced in paise: Sarvam’s Raghavan
articles.summary: Sarvam AI’s Vivek Raghavan urges India to build a full AI stack locally, warning of “digital colony” risks and calling for low-cost, paise-priced inference.
articles.body: Bengaluru: India risks becoming a digital colony if it continues to export its data and import intelligence, Sarvam AI co-founder Vivek Raghavan said, calling for the country to build capabilities across the AI technology stack instead of depending on global models and infrastructure.“Today, we are exporting our data and importing intelligence,” Raghavan said at Bengaluru Tech Summit 2026 on Tuesday. Drawing a parallel with colonial-era trade, when India exported cotton and imported cloth, he cautioned that the country could face similar dependence in the digital economy.When users interact with global AI models, their data leaves the country and helps improve models developed elsewhere. As these models get better, more users gravitate towards them, reinforcing the cycle. “A lot of people are very proud to say that India is the largest user of ChatGPT. But this is not a good thing,” he said.In June, Sarvam raised $234 million in a funding round led by HCLTech and Bessemer Venture Partners, taking its valuation to $1.5 billion and making it one of India’s newest AI unicorns.Raghavan said technological sovereignty requires India to build capabilities across five layers — compute, data and evaluations, models, harnesses and applications. While the country may not yet be close to manufacturing advanced AI chips, it should ensure that GPUs and cloud infrastructure are located in India, with sensitive and regulated workloads hosted and operated by Indian entities.He called for building Indic datasets and benchmarks to improve model performance in Indian languages and on tasks relevant to the country. India should use the best open-weight models while also developing its own, he said. Open weights alone do not guarantee sovereignty if the training data cannot be audited.Raghavan said Sarvam had built a 105-billion-parameter model with a team of about 20 people, most of them under 25, and was working towards developing a trillion-parameter model from scratch.He stressed that AI products for India must be designed around affordability, scale, local languages and voice. The price of 1GB of mobile data has fallen 97%, from Rs 287 in 2014 to Rs 9 in 2025. Over the same period, monthly data consumption per subscriber surged from 61.66MB to 24GB, nearly 399 times, while broadband connections rose 15.7 times to 94.4 crore, according to figures cited from Department of Telecommunications.Raghavan said AI inference would need a similar affordability model. “A Rs 200 recharge and an Rs 8,000 handset set the ceiling for what a conversation can cost. Inference priced per token in dollars cannot serve this market; it has to be priced per conversation, at Indian scale,” he said.With nearly one billion active internet users and about 500 million people still outside the internet, voice will be crucial to expanding access. AI interfaces must work across India’s 22 scheduled languages and thousands of dialects, rather than expect users to adapt to technology.Raghavan said the larger goal was “universal basic intelligence”, giving every citizen access to an AI agent that understands their language, represents their interests and helps them access services and build skills.Money habits form by age 7.
